title: The Stress Posture
hook: Stress has a shape, and many men have worn it for years: shoulders up, jaw set, breath high, the body braced for a blow that never comes.
why:
Stress is the most common state you will ever read, in yourself and in others, and it is the easiest to misread. A colleague braced for a difficult call looks hostile. A father worried about money looks short-tempered with his children. A man carrying months of strain stops noticing that his shoulders have been up near his ears since spring. The body announces stress clearly, and the announcement is heard as something else.

This first chapter of Part II teaches the shape of stress: what the body does when it prepares for a threat, why that preparation shows as a particular posture, what happens when the preparation never switches off, and how to read stress in someone else against their baseline and their situation. It ends with what actually helps a stressed person, which turns out to have less to do with telling them to relax and more to do with giving them some control. As with every chapter in this part, the aim is recognition and a kind response, never a diagnosis.

teach.h: Stress is the body getting ready.
teach.p:
When a person perceives a threat or a demand they are not sure they can meet, two systems respond. The sympathetic nervous system acts within seconds: the heart speeds up, breathing quickens and rises into the chest, blood flows to the large muscles, the pupils widen and the palms may sweat. A slower hormonal system follows over minutes, releasing cortisol, which mobilises energy and keeps the body ready.

None of this is a malfunction. It is the body preparing to act, and in short bursts it helps: before a match, a presentation or a difficult conversation, a degree of arousal sharpens attention and gives energy. The chapter on reading yourself under stress, in Part VI, described how reappraising that arousal as readiness can help.

Much of the preparation is visible. Breathing becomes faster and higher, visible in the shoulders and upper chest. Skin may pale or flush. Hands may tremble slightly, or grip something. Movements become quicker and less fluid, or the body goes unusually still. The voice tends to rise and tighten, as the chapter on voice described. The face may tighten around the jaw and the brows.

The difficulty for a reader is that the same preparation happens whatever the threat. A man bracing for criticism, a man worried about his daughter's health, a man late for a train and a man about to lie all mobilise the same systems. Stress tells you that something is being demanded of the body. It does not tell you what.

When you see the signs of stress, the useful first thought is not *what is he hiding?* but *what is he facing?*
teach.disconfirm: If people facing very different kinds of demand, a deadline, a frightening diagnosis, a lie they were telling, showed clearly different bodily signs, you could tell the cause from the body. The physiology described here is largely the same across causes, which is why the question has to be asked.
teach.pullQuote: Stress tells you that something is being demanded of the body. It does not tell you what.

teach.p:
In 1939 Carney Landis and William Hunt filmed people's reactions to a sudden loud noise, a gunshot fired behind them, at high speed. They described a consistent startle pattern that unfolds in a fraction of a second: the eyes blink, the head jerks forward and down, the shoulders rise, the arms pull in and bend, the trunk flexes and the knees bend slightly. It is a protective crouch, the body folding around its softest parts.

A milder version of that crouch is the posture of ongoing stress. The shoulders lift towards the ears, the head drops forward, the arms stay close to the body, the jaw tightens and the breath stays high. Measurements of the trapezius, the large muscle across the top of the shoulders, have repeatedly found its activity rising during purely mental stress, such as timed arithmetic or a stressful interview, with no physical effort involved at all.

Many people hold a version of this posture for hours a day without noticing. They notice the effects instead: a stiff neck in the evening, a headache, a jaw that aches in the morning from clenching overnight. The chapter on reading yourself under stress described how to find your own signature; this chapter asks you to see the same shape in others.

In someone else, look at the line from the ears to the shoulders, the set of the jaw, and where the breath moves. Shoulders that have crept up, a jaw held tight and breathing high in the chest form a small cluster that often means a body braced for something. Compare it, as always, with how this person usually holds themselves.
teach.disconfirm: If the muscles across the shoulders did not become more active during purely mental stress, the link between stress and the raised-shoulder posture would be weak. Studies measuring those muscles have repeatedly found that they do, though people differ in how much.

teach.h: When stress does not switch off.
teach.p:
The stress response is built to turn on quickly and off again when the demand passes. The neuroscientist Bruce McEwen described the process of adapting to demands as allostasis, and in a widely cited paper in 1998 he described what happens when the systems are activated too often, for too long, or fail to switch off: a cumulative wear on the body that he called allostatic load. Over time it is linked to raised blood pressure, disturbed sleep, changes in immune function and a higher risk of several illnesses.

For a reader, chronic stress changes the baseline itself. A person who has been under strain for months may not show the sharp changes of acute stress, because the stressed state has become their normal. Their shoulders are always up. Their sleep is always short. Their temper is always shorter than it used to be. Measured against their recent baseline, nothing has changed. Measured against how they were a year ago, a great deal has.

This is why it is worth keeping a longer memory of the people close to you. Notice when a friend's laugh has become rare, when a colleague who used to linger at lunch now eats at his desk, when your partner's shoulders have not come down in weeks. Chronic stress hides in the slow drift of a baseline, and the people best placed to see it are the ones who knew the person before.

Chronic stress is also the ground in which other difficulties grow, including low mood, anxiety and burnout, which later chapters in this part describe. Noticing it early matters.
teach.disconfirm: If people under long-term strain showed the same sharp changes as people under sudden stress, chronic stress would be easy to see against a recent baseline. In practice it tends to shift the baseline itself, which is why comparing with how someone was months ago matters.

teach.h: Read stress against the person and the situation.
teach.p:
Because the stress response is so common and so general, reading it well depends on everything this book has taught about baselines, clusters and context.

Start with the situation. Many situations make almost everyone stressed: a job interview, a hospital waiting room, a court, a first date, an argument, a border crossing. Stress in those settings is normal, and it tells you about the situation, not the person. The chapter on deception explained how often stress under questioning is misread as guilt.

Then the person. Some people show stress readily, with flushed faces and quick speech; others go still and quiet. Some are anxious by temperament, and look stressed in situations others find easy. A person's own baseline in similar situations tells you far more than any general picture.

Then the cluster and the timing, as the chapter on clusters described. Shoulders rising, breath quickening and hands finding something to hold, all within a few seconds of a particular topic, tell you that the topic carries weight for this person. One of those signs alone, at no particular moment, tells you very little.

And then a word of caution that applies to all of Part II. Signs of stress are not a diagnosis of anything. They are a reason to wonder what someone is carrying, and sometimes a reason to ask. If you find yourself concluding that someone has an anxiety problem or is heading for a breakdown from what you have seen of their body, you have gone further than the evidence can take you.

Stress in a stressful place is the place talking. Stress that is new for this person is the person talking.
teach.disconfirm: If signs of stress in high-pressure settings turned out to predict people's general wellbeing as well as signs that were unusual for them, situation would matter less than this block claims. Compare a few people you know in stressful and ordinary settings before deciding.

teach.h: Uncontrollable and unpredictable stress hurts most.
teach.p:
Not all stress is equal. In the early 1970s David Glass and Jerome Singer exposed people to loud, unpleasant bursts of noise while they worked. Noise that came at random intervals had worse after-effects than noise at regular intervals: afterwards, people gave up sooner on frustrating puzzles and made more errors. Remarkably, giving people a switch that would stop the noise reduced the after-effects, even when they never pressed it. The sense of control was enough.

The review by Sally Dickerson and Margaret Kemeny described in Part VI found something similar in the body's hormonal response: stress that people could not control, especially when combined with being judged by others, produced the largest rises in cortisol.

This has direct consequences for how you treat a stressed person. Much of what makes a situation stressful is not the demand itself but the lack of control over it and the uncertainty about what will happen. A person waiting for news, unsure when it will come, often suffers more than a person who knows bad news is coming at three o'clock.

So the most useful things you can offer are often information and choice. Tell people what will happen and when. Give them options, even small ones: *Would you rather talk now or after lunch?* Let them control what they can, such as the pace, the place, who else is present. A manager delivering difficult news can reduce its harm considerably by being predictable, clear and respectful of the person's control over what happens next.

A switch you never press can still make the noise bearable.
teach.disconfirm: If people given information and small choices during stressful situations fared no better than those given none, control would matter less than this block suggests. Notice the difference the next time you can offer someone a choice in a hard moment.

teach.h: Stress also pulls people towards each other.
teach.p:
The phrase *fight or flight* suggests that stress makes people aggressive or makes them run. In 2000 Shelley Taylor and colleagues proposed another pattern, which they called tend-and-befriend: under stress, people often turn towards others, protecting those they care for and seeking company and support. Taylor suggested the pattern might be especially strong in women.

Later research found it in men too. In 2012 Bernadette von Dawans, Markus Heinrichs and colleagues put men through a stressful group task, public speaking and mental arithmetic in front of evaluators, and then had them play games involving trust and sharing with real money. The stressed men were more trusting, more trustworthy and more willing to share than men who had not been stressed, and no more aggressive.

For a reader, this changes what stress can look like. A colleague who suddenly seeks your company, lingers at your desk, asks to join you for lunch or calls more often than usual may be reaching for the support that stress makes people want. A man who becomes unexpectedly warm or talkative in a crisis may be tending and befriending, not avoiding the problem.

It also suggests what helps. Company is one of the oldest buffers against stress, as the chapter on the quiet body described. Being available, without pressing, is often more useful than any advice.

When stress makes someone reach for you, let them find you there.
teach.disconfirm: If stressed people consistently withdrew from others rather than seeking them, the tend-and-befriend pattern would not hold. The research suggests both responses occur, and that approaching others is more common than the phrase fight or flight implies.

teach.p:
Put this together and a few practical habits emerge. First, notice before you react. When someone seems short, cold or hostile, check for the shape of stress, the raised shoulders, the high breath, the tight jaw, before deciding it is about you.

Second, lower the load where you can. Slow your own pace and lower your voice, as the chapters on voice and reading the room described; a stressed person often matches what is around them. Remove demands that can wait. Do not add a second difficult topic to a conversation that is already hard.

Third, offer information and choice. Tell people what will happen, when, and what they can decide. Fourth, ask simply and without diagnosis: *You seem to have a lot on. Anything I can take off your plate?* is better than *You look really stressed*, which can feel like being inspected.

Fifth, avoid *relax* and *calm down*. They place the burden back on the person and usually make things worse.

And sixth, know where your role ends. Stress that persists for weeks, that disrupts sleep night after night, that comes with panic, hopelessness or a person talking about not being able to go on, needs more than a kind colleague. Encourage them to see a doctor, and if you are worried about their safety, the crisis resources in this app are one tap away. The later chapters of this part describe these situations in more detail.
teach.disconfirm: If lowering demands, offering choices and asking simply made stressed people no more at ease with you than your usual approach, these habits would not help in your setting. Try them with one person over a fortnight and ask them how it felt.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Shoulders crept up to the ears, unnoticed for weeks.
poseGallery.annotation: The bracing posture is a small version of the startle crouch. Many people hold it for hours without knowing.

poseGallery.doCaption: 'Would you rather talk now, or after lunch?'
poseGallery.annotation: Telling someone to relax adds a demand. Offering a choice gives back a little control, which is what most eases stress.

poseGallery.doCaption: Seeing the braced body, and staying nearby.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Reading a stressed colleague's shortness as hostility.
poseGallery.annotation: Stress often looks like coldness from outside. Many people under stress want company, even when they do not ask for it.

poseGallery.doCaption: Taking demands off the table until it has passed.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Adding one more demand to a hard conversation.
poseGallery.annotation: Lowering the load is often more useful than any advice. One hard thing at a time is enough.

caseStudy:
Gary, forty-eight, manages a warehouse team. Over the autumn, one of his best supervisors, Paul, becomes difficult to work with. He snaps at the night shift, answers Gary's questions in single words and once walks out of a meeting. Two people complain. Gary's first instinct is a formal warning.

Before he decides, he watches Paul for a few days. He notices that Paul's shoulders are up almost all the time now, that he rubs his neck constantly, that he eats lunch standing up and that he checks his phone every few minutes. When Gary thinks back to last year, he remembers a man who leaned on the loading-bay door, laughing with the drivers. The change has been slow. Nobody noticed it happening.

Gary asks Paul to walk the yard with him, side by side, at a quiet time. He does not mention the complaints first. He says Paul seems to have a lot on and asks whether there is anything Gary could take off his plate. Paul is quiet for a long time. Then he says his father has dementia and has moved in with him and his wife, and that he has not slept a full night since September. He keeps checking his phone in case of a fall.

Gary gives him two things. He moves Paul off the rotating night shifts for three months, so his hours are predictable. And he agrees that Paul can take calls about his father at any time without asking. He also mentions the company's employee assistance line and suggests Paul talk to his doctor about his sleep.

The complaints stop. Paul's shoulders are not down yet, but by Christmas he is leaning on the loading-bay door again, now and then.
observe: Look at the line from the ears to the shoulders of three people you see today, and notice whose shoulders have risen and when.
Notice one moment when someone's shortness with you might have been the shape of stress rather than anything about you.
Notice where your own shoulders, jaw and breath are right now, and again at the end of a difficult day.

drills.name: Shoulder Check
steps: Set three reminders on your phone for different times tomorrow.
At each one, notice where your shoulders are without moving them.
Notice your jaw and where your breath is moving in the chest or belly.
Breathe out slowly and let your shoulders drop as far as they will go.
Write down how far they dropped each time, as a rough measure of how much you were bracing.

drills.name: Baseline Drift
steps: Choose two people you see often and recall how they were a year ago: their posture, their laugh, their pace.
Write down how they are now on the same points.
Mark any slow changes you had not noticed until now.
For each change, write two possible causes, at least one about their circumstances.
Decide whether any change is worth a gentle question, and write the question.

drills.name: Situation or Person
steps: Over a week, note three occasions when someone seemed stressed.
For each, write whether the situation was one that would stress most people.
Note whether the stress was unusual for this particular person.
Mark which readings were about the situation and which about the person.
Write one sentence about how this changes what you would do.

drills.name: Offer a Switch
steps: Think of someone you will see this week who is under pressure.
Identify one piece of information you could give them about what will happen and when.
Identify one small choice you could offer them.
Offer both in your next conversation, simply and without comment.
Note how they responded.

drills.name: What Not to Say
steps: Write down the phrases you tend to use when someone is stressed, such as calm down or don't worry.
For each, write how it might feel to hear it when you are stressed yourself.
Write a replacement for each that offers information, choice or company instead.
Say the replacements aloud until they sound natural.
Use one of them this week and note what happened.

quiz.q: A colleague is short with you, shoulders up and breathing high, just before an important meeting. What does that tell you?
options: That he is angry with you about something and is trying to hide it
That he has an anxiety problem and should be encouraged to get help
That something is being demanded of him; the posture does not say what
That he is preparing to say something in the meeting that is not true
quiz.explain: The stress response is much the same whatever the demand. It tells you the body is getting ready for something, which before an important meeting is ordinary. It does not tell you the cause, and it is not a diagnosis.

quiz.q: What did Glass and Singer find when people working through unpredictable bursts of noise were given a switch to stop it?
options: The after-effects of the noise were reduced, even if they never used the switch
The noise bothered them more, because the switch kept reminding them of it
The switch made no difference to how well they performed afterwards
People pressed the switch at once and so heard almost none of the noise
quiz.explain: A sense of control reduced the harm of the stressor even when it was not exercised. Offering people information and small choices draws on the same principle.

quiz.q: What did McEwen mean by allostatic load?
options: The amount of work a person can carry before they feel any stress
The level of cortisol present in the blood first thing in the morning
A sudden, short burst of stress that improves a person's performance
The wear on the body when stress systems are activated too often or too long
quiz.explain: Short bursts of stress help us adapt. When the systems stay on or switch on too often, the cumulative wear is linked to poor sleep, raised blood pressure and illness, and it can shift a person's baseline so the change is hard to see.

quiz.q: A supervisor who used to be relaxed has become short-tempered over several months, with his shoulders always up. What fits this chapter?
options: Issue a formal warning, since his behaviour has been going on for months
Compare him with how he was a year ago, and ask what he is carrying
Tell him that he looks very stressed and should try to relax more
Leave it alone, since his recent baseline shows that nothing has changed
quiz.explain: Chronic stress shifts the baseline, so comparing with his recent self shows little. A longer memory reveals the drift, and a simple question about his load, ideally side by side, is the kind response.

quiz.q: What did von Dawans and colleagues find when men were put through a stressful public-speaking task?
options: They became more aggressive and less willing to trust anyone else
They withdrew from the others and refused to take part in the games
They became more trusting and more willing to share with others
They behaved in exactly the same way as men who were not stressed
quiz.explain: Stress increased positive social behaviour in men and did not increase aggression. Stress can draw people towards others, so a stressed colleague seeking your company may be looking for support.

quiz.q: You need to give a team member bad news about a reorganisation that affects her. What fits this chapter?
options: Tell her clearly what will happen and when, and what she can still choose
Wait until the very last moment, so that she has less time to worry about it
Keep the details vague, so that she can get used to the idea gradually
Tell her to stay calm, and that worrying about it will not change anything
quiz.explain: Uncertainty and lack of control make stress worse. Being clear about what will happen and when, and giving her what choices you can, reduces the harm of news you cannot change.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific person in your life who has been under strain recently. Describe how their body has changed, as behaviour: their shoulders, their breath, their pace, their temper, compared with how they were before. Then describe one thing that is outside their control and one thing that is unpredictable for them. What information or small choice could you offer them this week, and how would you offer it without making them feel watched?
reflection.guidance: Many people find that they had read the person's strain as a change in personality before reading it as stress. Try to describe the body before the mood. The last question is the useful one. Information and choice often help more than reassurance, and they can be offered without ever mentioning stress at all.

failureMode: The commonest failure is to read stress as hostility, coldness or guilt, and to respond to the person as if they were against you. The second is to miss chronic stress altogether, because it shifts the baseline slowly and nothing seems to change from week to week. The third is to respond with *relax* or *calm down*, which adds a demand and usually makes things worse. And the fourth is to go too far in the other direction, turning a few visible signs into a judgment about someone's mental health. Stress is a reason to wonder what someone is carrying, and sometimes to ask. When it lasts, disrupts sleep, or comes with hopelessness, the right response is to encourage a doctor's help, not to diagnose it yourself.

watch.title: How stress affects your body
watch.notice: An animated lesson on what stress does inside the body. Connect it to what shows on the outside: raised shoulders, shallow breathing, a tight jaw.

reviewPrompt: Check your own shoulders, jaw and breath three times this week, and offer one stressed person a piece of information or a small choice.
